query: Traditional fusion welding can be unsuitable for repairing certain damaged high-value components because their physical and microstructural characteristics create a risk of hot cracking. For preventing or delaying surface-defect initiation, earlier work has used PVD, CVD, electroplating, and thermal diffusion to improve hardness and resistance to wear and corrosion, but these approaches can involve costly deposition equipment, pollution, or long processing times. Under the constraints of avoiding whole-part replacement and limiting these drawbacks, what intervention could repair or improve the surface for service in aggressive environments? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, the operative mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to traditional fusion-welding repair and an untreated surface, its processing and service boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Using spark plasma sintering (SPS) to consolidate high-entropy alloy powders at elevated temperatures to produce electrospark-deposition (ESD) electrodes, followed by depositing a multi‐layer (e.g., six-layer) coating, will yield a coating with improved densification, microstructural homogenization, and increased hardness that better resists hot cracking and degrades less under aggressive environments compared to traditional fusion welding repairs and untreated substrates.
generation.material_initial_state: Mechanically alloyed CrFeNiMo, Co0.5CrFeNiMo, and Al0.5CrFeNiMo metallic powders (milled for 30 h with N-heptane and sieved to ≤80 µm) with a polished and degreased low-carbon C1018 steel substrate.
generation.intervention: Consolidation of the HEA powders by SPS at higher temperatures (with testing at 950/1000/1050 °C for CrFeNiMo, 900/950/1000 °C for Co0.5CrFeNiMo, and 850/900/950 °C for Al0.5CrFeNiMo) to create machinable ESD electrodes, which are then used to deposit either 3-layer or 6-layer coatings on the C1018 steel substrate.
generation.conditions: SPS processing at 50 MPa pressure, 50 °C/min heating, 5 min dwell, and 30 °C/min cooling in graphite tooling; ESD performed under an Ar shield (5 L/min) with the electrode held at approximately 45° and processing parameters (e.g., for CrFeNiMo: 30 µF/100 V/360 Hz) with deposition rates from 1.86 to 2.71 mm/s; tests conducted in lab conditions before exposure to simulated aggressive environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Elevated SPS temperatures lead to greater particle diffusion, homogenization, and densification with reduced porosity, while the ESD process produces chemically mixed HEA layers whose structural integrity (continuity, reduced porosity) is determined by the number of layers and rapid solidification effects (which may also induce oxidation and microfissuring in thicker deposits).
generation.mechanism: The higher-temperature SPS improves pore closure and microstructural refinement, yielding electrodes that transfer material more effectively during ESD. The enhanced deposition, especially from a 6-layer approach, promotes more complete surface coverage and increased hardness. This refined structure is expected to reduce susceptibility to hot cracking while also delivering better wear and corrosion resistance in aggressive environments compared to traditional fusion welding repairs.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to lower-temperature SPS samples and 3-layer coatings, the 6-layer coatings produced from higher-temperature SPS electrodes will exhibit improved homogeneity, reduced porosity, and increased hardness. These improvements are expected to offer enhanced resistance against surface defects such as hot cracking and provide some improvement in corrosion and wear performance when operating in aggressive environments.
generation.baseline: Lower-temperature SPS electrodes (950 °C for CrFeNiMo, 900 °C for Co0.5CrFeNiMo, 850 °C for Al0.5CrFeNiMo) and 3-layer ESD coatings on polished C1018 steel, as well as the untreated polished steel substrate.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies specifically to the tested mechanically alloyed HEA compositions under the given SPS and ESD processing parameters. The beneficial effects are assumed up to the six-layer deposition limit, beyond which additional layers do not significantly improve coating mass or integrity and may exacerbate oxidation and microfissuring. The predicted improvements in corrosion and wear resistance remain to be validated under simulated aggressive (e.g., geothermal) conditions.
generation.uncertainty: While improved densification and hardness are predicted with higher SPS temperatures and thicker ESD layers, there is uncertainty regarding the extent of oxidation, microfissuring, and real-world corrosion/wear performance under aggressive environmental exposures.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare samples with SPS consolidation at both lower (e.g., 950 °C) and higher temperatures (e.g., 1050 °C) for the respective alloys. Deposit both 3-layer and 6-layer coatings using ESD onto polished C1018 steel substrates. Evaluate coating morphology and integrity using SEM with EDS elemental mapping, assess phase structures and lattice distortion via XRD, measure coating density and porosity with Archimedes method, and determine hardness using Vickers HV2/15 testing. Finally, subject the coatings to simulated aggressive environmental conditions (e.g., corrosion and wear tests) to compare performance against traditional fusion welded repairs and untreated substrates.
measurements: SEM with EDS for porosity, cracks, and phase continuity
XRD for phase identification and lattice distortions
Archimedes density measurements for porosity evaluation
Mass measurements per layer to confirm the deposition limit
Corrosion and wear testing under simulated aggressive conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be rejected if the 6-layer coatings produced from higher-temperature SPS electrodes do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in densification, reduced porosity, increased hardness, and superior performance (corrosion/wear resistance) compared to both lower-temperature SPS/3-layer coatings and traditional fusion welding repairs under the same test conditions.
